dryRun.title: Rotate a 3 × 3 matrix 90° clockwise
rows: the first row 1 2 3 is now the last column
dryRun.note: Rotation is two simple moves: transpose, then reverse every row. No special case for each cell.

think.q:
const m = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
console.log(m[1][0], m.length, m[0].length)
why: m[1] is the second row [3, 4], and [0] of it is 3. m.length counts rows (2) and m[0].length counts columns (2).
The row index always comes first: m[row][col].

think.q:
const g = new Array(2).fill([])
g[0].push(1)
console.log(g[1].length)
why: fill([]) puts the same empty array into every slot. A push into row 0 also shows up in row 1.
Fix: Array.from({ length: 2 }, () => []), which makes a fresh row each time.

think.q:
const m = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
const t = m[0].map((_, c) => m.map((row) => row[c]))
console.log(JSON.stringify(t))
why: For every column c, the code reads that column from top to bottom and makes it a new row. This is a transpose.
A 2 × 3 matrix becomes 3 × 2.

think.q: A matrix has R rows and C columns. How long does it take to visit every cell once?
why: Every one of the R × C cells is touched once. That is O(R * C).
If the matrix is square with n rows, this is O(n²).

think.q: You are walking a matrix in spiral order with four boundaries (top, bottom, left, right). You have just walked the top row from left to right. What do you do next?
opts: Move the top boundary down by one
Move the bottom boundary up by one
Start again from the first cell
why: That row is finished, so the top boundary shrinks by one. Then you walk down the right column, and so on.
Each pass shrinks one boundary. The walk ends when the boundaries cross.

try.task: Write rotate90(matrix). Return a new matrix rotated 90° clockwise. The matrix may not be square. The input must stay unchanged.
try.hint: Transpose, then reverse each row. In one go: new row c is column c read from the bottom to the top.

checks.verify: const m = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]; rotate90(m); assert(JSON.stringify(m) === "[[1,2],[3,4]]", "input was changed")
assert(JSON.stringify(rotate90([])) === "[]" && JSON.stringify(rotate90([[5]])) === "[[5]]", "edge cases")

takeaway.key: A matrix is an array of arrays: reading a cell is O(1), visiting all cells is O(rows × columns), and rotate = transpose + reverse each row.
mistakes: Building rows with fill([]), so all rows are the same array.
Mixing up the order: it is m[row][col], not m[col][row].
Forgetting empty or non-square matrices.
Off-by-one errors when the spiral boundaries shrink.

dryRun.title: Remove duplicates from [3, 1, 3, 2, 1], keeping the first appearance
dryRun.note: The question at every step is one yes or no: "have I seen this value?". The set answers it in O(1), and the order of first appearance is kept.

think.q: console.log([...new Set([3, 1, 3, 2, 1])].join(','))
why: A Set keeps each value once and remembers the order in which values were first added: 3, 1, 2.
Trap: expecting a sorted result. A Set does not sort.

think.q: console.log(new Set([0, -0]).size)
why: A Set treats 0 and -0 as the same value, so only one item remains.
Sets compare with "same value zero". It also treats NaN as equal to itself, unlike ===.

think.q:
const seen = []
for (const x of arr) {
  if (!seen.includes(x)) seen.push(x)
}

What is the time of this "remove duplicates" code for n items?
why: includes scans the whole seen array on every round. Scanning inside a loop is O(n²).
With a Set, has is O(1) on average and the same code is O(n).

think.q:
const a = new Set([1, 2, 3])
const b = new Set([2, 3, 4])
console.log([...a].filter((x) => b.has(x)).join(","))
why: The code keeps the items of a that are also in b. That is the intersection: 2 and 3.
Each b.has is O(1), so the whole thing is O(n).

think.q:
const s = new Set([1])
for (const x of s) {
  if (x < 3) s.add(x + 1)
}
console.log([...s].join(","))
why: A Set loop also visits items that are added while it runs. It sees 1, adds 2, sees 2, adds 3, sees 3 and stops.
Changing a collection while you loop over it is a common source of surprises.

try.task: Write intersect(a, b). Return an array with the values that appear in both arrays. Each value must appear only once in the result. The order does not matter.
try.hint: Put one array in a Set. Walk the other array and keep the values that the first Set has. Put the kept values in a second Set to drop repeats.

checks.verify: assert(JSON.stringify(intersect([1, 2, 2, 1], [2, 2])) === "[2]", "expected [2]")
assert(JSON.stringify(intersect([4, 9, 5], [9, 4, 9, 8, 4]).sort()) === "[4,9]", "expected 4 and 9")
assert(intersect([1, 2], [3, 4]).length === 0, "expected an empty array")
assert(intersect([], [1]).length === 0 && intersect([1], []).length === 0, "expected empty arrays")

takeaway.key: A Set answers "is it in here?" in O(1) and drops duplicates for free. Use it instead of includes() inside a loop.
mistakes: Calling includes() on an array inside a loop, which makes it O(n²).
Expecting a Set to treat two equal-looking objects as the same value.
Expecting a Set to be sorted or to have index access. Spread it into an array first.
Changing the Set while looping over it.

dryRun.title: Insert 5, 9, 2, 13 into 4 buckets (bucket = key % 4)
rows: collision: the key joins the chain
collision again: a lookup of 13 must scan the chain
dryRun.note: Different keys can land in the same bucket. The bucket keeps a short list, and lookup scans only that list, not the whole table.

think.q: console.log(-3 % 4)
why: In JavaScript the result of % takes the sign of the left side, so -3 % 4 is -3, not 1.
A negative bucket index would break the table. Hash functions must make the number non-negative first.

think.q:
const buckets = [[], [], [], []]
for (const k of [5, 9, 2, 13]) buckets[k % 4].push(k)
console.log(buckets.map((b) => b.length).join(","))
why: 5, 9 and 13 all have remainder 1, so bucket 1 holds three keys. 2 goes to bucket 2.
Uneven buckets are normal. A good hash function keeps them close to even.

think.q: A terrible hash function sends every key to the same bucket. What does a lookup cost with n keys?
why: All n keys sit in one chain, so a lookup may scan all of them: O(n).
This is why O(1) is only the average case, and why the hash function matters.

think.q: Why do we double the number of buckets when the table gets too full (a high load factor)?
opts: To keep the chains short, so lookups stay close to O(1)
To avoid calling the hash function
why: Load factor is items divided by buckets. If it grows, chains grow and lookups slow down. More buckets spread the keys out again.
Resizing costs O(n) once, but it is rare, just like a dynamic array.

think.q: A set(key, value) always pushes a new entry into the bucket and never checks whether the key is already there. You call set("a", 1) and then set("a", 2). What goes wrong?
opts: Nothing: both values are stored correctly
get("a") can return the old value 1, because the first match wins
why: The chain now holds two entries for "a". A lookup that stops at the first match returns the old value.
Fix: search the chain first. If the key exists, update it. Otherwise push a new entry.

try.task: Write createHashMap(). It returns an object with set(key, value), get(key), has(key) and delete(key) for string keys. Build it from an array of buckets with chaining. Do not use Map or plain objects as storage.
try.hint: Use 8 buckets, each an array of [key, value] pairs. Hash a string by looping over its characters: h = (h * 31 + code) % 8. In set, look for the key in the bucket first and update it if found.

checks.verify: const m = createHashMap(); m.set("a", 1); m.set("b", 2); assert(m.get("a") === 1 && m.get("b") === 2, "get should return the stored values")
const m = createHashMap(); assert(m.get("zzz") === undefined && m.has("zzz") === false, "missing key")

checks.t: setting the same key again updates it
checks.verify: const m = createHashMap(); m.set("a", 1); m.set("a", 2); assert(m.get("a") === 2, "expected the updated value 2")
const m = createHashMap(); m.set("a", 1); assert(m.delete("a") === true && m.has("a") === false && m.delete("a") === false, "delete should remove once")
const m = createHashMap(); for (let i = 0; i < 50; i++) m.set("k" + i, i); let ok = true; for (let i = 0; i < 50; i++) if (m.get("k" + i) !== i) ok = false; assert(ok, "every key must be found")

takeaway.key: A hash table is an array of buckets: hash the key, take % size, then search the short chain. Collisions and a high load factor are the two things to handle.
mistakes: Using a negative number as a bucket index, because % can return a negative value.
Pushing a new entry when the key already exists, instead of updating it.
Never resizing, so chains grow and lookups slow down.
Believing the O(1) is guaranteed. It is the average case.

dryRun.title: Remove B from A ⇄ B ⇄ C when you hold node B
rows: A → C, but C.prev still points to B
dryRun.note: Two links must change, one on each side. No walk from the head is needed because B already knows both neighbours.

think.q:
const a = { val: 'a', prev: null, next: null }
const b = { val: 'b', prev: a, next: null }
a.next = b
console.log(b.prev.val, a.next.val, String(a.prev))
why: b.prev is a, a.next is b, and a.prev is null because a is the head.
Every link in a doubly linked list has a partner in the other direction.

think.q:
const a = { val: 1, prev: null, next: null }
const b = { val: 2, prev: a, next: null }
const c = { val: 3, prev: b, next: null }
a.next = b
b.next = c
b.prev.next = b.next
b.next.prev = b.prev
console.log(a.next.val, c.prev.val)
why: After the two lines, a.next is c (value 3) and c.prev is a (value 1). Node b is out of the list.
Both directions agree again.

think.q: You already hold a reference to the node to delete. How do singly and doubly linked lists compare?
opts: Singly: O(n), because you must find the previous node. Doubly: O(1)
why: A singly linked node does not know its previous node, so you walk from the head to find it. A doubly linked node has prev.
This is the whole reason for the extra pointer.

think.q: You remove b (between a and c) with only b.prev.next = b.next. What is wrong afterwards?
opts: c.prev still points to b, so walking backward from c visits the removed node
why: Walking forward is fine: a.next is now c. But c.prev still points to b, so the list is broken in the other direction.
Always update both links.

think.q: An LRU cache moves a used item to the front of the list in O(1). Which two things make that possible?
opts: A sorted array and binary search
A hash map to find the node, and prev / next to unlink it
why: The map finds the node instantly. With prev and next you cut it out and put it at the front with a few pointer changes.
A singly linked list could not unlink the node without a walk.

try.task: Write removeNode(node). The node is part of a doubly linked list (each node is { val, prev, next }). Unlink it so its neighbours point to each other. The node may be the head, the tail, or the only node.
examples: A ⇄ B ⇄ C, removeNode(B)  // A ⇄ C
removeNode on the head  // the next node becomes the head
try.hint: If node.prev exists, set node.prev.next = node.next. If node.next exists, set node.next.prev = node.prev. Guard each one, because the head has no prev and the tail has no next.

checks.verify: { const mk = (v) => { const ns = v.map((x) => ({ val: x, prev: null, next: null })); ns.forEach((n, i) => { n.prev = ns[i - 1] || null; n.next = ns[i + 1] || null }); return ns }; const fwd = (h) => { const o = []; while (h) { o.push(h.val); h = h.next } return o }; const bwd = (t) => { const o = []; while (t) { o.push(t.val); t = t.prev } return o }; const ns = mk([1, 2, 3]); removeNode(ns[1]); assert(JSON.stringify(fwd(ns[0])) === "[1,3]" && JSON.stringify(bwd(ns[2])) === "[3,1]", "both directions must skip the removed node") }

{ const mk = (v) => { const ns = v.map((x) => ({ val: x, prev: null, next: null })); ns.forEach((n, i) => { n.prev = ns[i - 1] || null; n.next = ns[i + 1] || null }); return ns }; const ns = mk([1, 2, 3]); removeNode(ns[0]); assert(ns[1].prev === null && ns[1].next === ns[2], "node 2 must become the head") }

{ const mk = (v) => { const ns = v.map((x) => ({ val: x, prev: null, next: null })); ns.forEach((n, i) => { n.prev = ns[i - 1] || null; n.next = ns[i + 1] || null }); return ns }; const ns = mk([1, 2, 3]); removeNode(ns[2]); assert(ns[1].next === null && ns[1].prev === ns[0], "node 2 must become the tail") }
{ const n = { val: 1, prev: null, next: null }; removeNode(n); assert(n.prev === null && n.next === null, "should not crash") }

takeaway.key: A doubly linked list adds prev, so removing a node you already hold costs O(1): fix two links, one on each side.
mistakes: Updating only one direction, which leaves the list broken the other way.
Not guarding the head and the tail, where prev or next is null.
Leaving the removed node still pointing into the list.
Forgetting the extra memory: every node stores two pointers.

dryRun.title: Floyd on 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → back to 2
dryRun.note: Slow moves one node, fast moves two. Inside a cycle, fast gains one node per step on slow, so they must meet.

think.q:
const a = { val: 1, next: null }
const b = { val: 2, next: null }
const c = { val: 3, next: null }
a.next = b
b.next = c
c.next = a
let cur = a, out = ''
for (let i = 0; i < 7; i++) {
  out += cur.val
  cur = cur.next
}
console.log(out)
why: The last node points back to the first, so the walk wraps around: 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, 1.
No % length is needed. The wrap is built into the links.

think.q: You walk a circular list with while (cur) { cur = cur.next }. What happens?
opts: It stops at the last node
It never ends, because no node has next === null
why: The loop stops only when cur is null. In a circle there is no null, so the loop runs forever.
This is also what a plain loop does when a normal list accidentally has a cycle.

think.q:
const n = [1, 2, 3, 4].map((v) => ({ val: v, next: null }))
n[0].next = n[1]
n[1].next = n[2]
n[2].next = n[3]
n[3].next = n[1]
let s = n[0], f = n[0], steps = 0
do {
  s = s.next
  f = f.next.next
  steps++
} while (s !== f)
console.log(steps, s.val)
why: This is the same list as the dry run. After 3 steps both pointers stand on the node with value 4.
They meet inside the cycle, not necessarily at its start.
think.exec:
const n = [1, 2, 3, 4].map((v) => ({ val: v, next: null }))
n[0].next = n[1]
n[1].next = n[2]
n[2].next = n[3]
n[3].next = n[1]
let s = n[0], f = n[0], steps = 0
do {
  s = s.next
  f = f.next.next
  steps++
} while (s !== f)
console.log(steps, s.val)

think.q: Why must the fast and slow pointers meet if there is a cycle?
opts: They always meet at the head
Inside the cycle, fast gains one node on slow each step, so the gap must reach zero
why: Fast moves two and slow moves one, so the distance between them changes by exactly one each step. It cannot jump over zero.
If there is no cycle, fast reaches null instead.

think.q: What is a simpler way to detect a cycle, and what does it cost?
opts: Remember visited nodes in a Set: O(n) space
Count the nodes first: O(1) space
Sort the nodes: O(n log n) space
why: If you reach a node you have already seen, there is a cycle. It is simple, but the Set holds up to n nodes.
Floyd needs only two pointers, so O(1) space.

try.task: Write hasCycle(head). Return true if following next from the head ever loops back, and false if it reaches null. Use two pointers and O(1) extra space.
try.hint: Start both pointers at the head. Move slow by one and fast by two. If they are the same node, return true. If fast or fast.next is null, there is no cycle.

checks.verify: assert(hasCycle(null) === false, "expected false")
{ const ns = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].map((v) => ({ val: v, next: null })); ns.forEach((n, i) => { n.next = ns[i + 1] || null }); assert(hasCycle(ns[0]) === false, "expected false") }
{ const n = { val: 1, next: null }; n.next = n; assert(hasCycle(n) === true, "expected true") }
{ const ns = [1, 2, 3, 4].map((v) => ({ val: v, next: null })); ns[0].next = ns[1]; ns[1].next = ns[2]; ns[2].next = ns[3]; ns[3].next = ns[1]; assert(hasCycle(ns[0]) === true, "expected true") }

checks.t: the whole list is a circle
checks.verify: { const ns = [1, 2, 3].map((v) => ({ val: v, next: null })); ns[0].next = ns[1]; ns[1].next = ns[2]; ns[2].next = ns[0]; assert(hasCycle(ns[0]) === true, "expected true") }

takeaway.key: A circular list has no null end, so never loop with while (cur) on it. Floyd's slow and fast pointers meet only if there is a cycle.
mistakes: Looping until null on a list that may be circular.
Moving the fast pointer without checking fast.next, which crashes on null.
Comparing node values instead of the nodes themselves.
Using a Set when O(1) space is possible.

dryRun.title: Window maximum of [1, 3, -1, -3, 5] with k = 3 (deque holds values, front is the max)
rows: [3]  (1 is smaller than 3, removed from the back)
[5]  (5 removed every smaller value from the back)
dryRun.note: The deque stays in decreasing order, so the front is always the maximum. New values clean the back, and stale values leave from the front.

think.q:
const d = [2, 3]
d.unshift(1)
d.push(4)
console.log(d.shift(), d.pop(), d.join(","))
why: After unshift(1) and push(4) the array is [1, 2, 3, 4]. shift removes the front (1), pop removes the back (4), and [2, 3] is left.
A deque works at both ends. In JS an array can act as one.
think.exec:
const d = [2, 3]
d.unshift(1)
d.push(4)
console.log(d.shift(), d.pop(), d.join(","))

think.q: Why is a plain JavaScript array a poor deque for a very large input?
opts: shift and unshift at the front can be O(n)
why: Working at the front can move every other item. A true deque does all four operations in O(1).
For interview-size inputs an array is fine. For huge ones, keep a head index or use a linked list.

think.q: You keep the maximum of a moving window in a deque of indexes. Which two removals do you need?
opts: From the front when an index leaves the window, and from the back when a new value is bigger than the last one
From the back when an index leaves the window
why: The front may hold an item that has left the window, so remove it. The back may hold values that can never be the maximum again, so remove them.
Two ends, two different reasons: that is why a queue or a stack alone is not enough.

think.q:
const dq = []
for (const x of [5, 3, 4, 1]) {
  while (dq.length && dq[dq.length - 1] < x) dq.pop()
  dq.push(x)
}
console.log(dq.join(","))
why: When 4 arrives, the smaller 3 at the back is removed, because 3 can never beat 4 again. Then 1 is smaller than 4, so it stays.
The result is in decreasing order: 5, 4, 1.

think.q: In the window-maximum deque we store indexes, not values. Why?
opts: So we can tell when the front item has left the window
why: An index tells us the position, so we can check index <= i - k and drop it. A value alone does not say where it came from.
The value is always one lookup away: nums[index].

try.task: Write windowMax(nums, k). Return the maximum of every window of k neighbouring numbers, from left to right. Use a deque of indexes so the work is O(n).
try.hint: For each index i: drop the front if it is <= i - k; drop from the back while nums[back] < nums[i]; push i; once i >= k - 1, the answer for this window is nums[front].

checks.verify: assert(JSON.stringify(windowMax([4, 2, 5], 1)) === "[4,2,5]", "expected [4,2,5]")
assert(JSON.stringify(windowMax([9, 8, 7, 6], 2)) === "[9,8,7]", "expected [9,8,7]")

checks.t: the window is the whole array
checks.verify: assert(JSON.stringify(windowMax([1, 2, 3], 3)) === "[3]", "expected [3]")
assert(JSON.stringify(windowMax([1], 1)) === "[1]", "expected [1]")

takeaway.key: A deque works at both ends in O(1): drop stale items from the front and weaker items from the back. It stays in order, so the front is the answer.
mistakes: Using Array.shift on a huge input and getting O(n) per call.
Storing values instead of indexes, so you cannot tell when an item left the window.
Forgetting to drop the front item when it leaves the window.
Being inconsistent with ties: decide whether an equal value stays or goes.

flags: hash-impl: the try-it hash only supports string keys and a fixed 8 buckets (no resize), on purpose. Resizing is a variation.
deque: the dry-run table is traced by hand (dry runs of concept lessons are not machine-run). The window-max try-it solution is machine-checked.
The old texts of deque and others contain interviewer framing. I did not rewrite them.
